title: Illumination: acquired knowledge helped by God's influence
source_text: XCIV. Ista vero mentis illuminatio ipsi nihil est aliud, quam notitiae quaedam ab externo concionatore, aut aliunde acceptae, & a Deo peculiari, & supernaturali influxu adjutae, ut aliquo modo jam ad salutem accommodatae sint. Observat enim Deum illis quos ordinaria ratione illuminat, non immittere novas species & ideas, quibus fiant cognitiones illae, quarum interventu mens eorum illustratur; sed cognitiones illas fieri per species humano modo acquisitas, & a concionatoribus, aut alia aliqua ratione excitatas, quibus Deus se inserit per suum influxum, ut cognitiones istae ad salutem plus minus accommodatae fiant, pro ratione majoris, vel minoris influxus. Quare, ex ejus sententia, Deum illuminare non aliud est, quam illo modo influxu suo cooperari ad tales cognitiones quibus voluntas excitatur.
pass_a_gloss: XCIV. That illumination of the mind is to him nothing other, than certain notions received from an external preacher, or from elsewhere, & helped by God's peculiar & supernatural influx, so that in some manner they are now accommodated to salvation. For he observes that God does not send into those whom he illuminates in the ordinary way new species & ideas, by which those cognitions come about, by whose intervention their mind is enlightened; but that those cognitions come about through species acquired in human manner, & excited by preachers, or in some other way, into which God inserts himself by his influx, that those cognitions may become more or less accommodated to salvation, according to the measure of the greater, or lesser influx. Wherefore, in his opinion, for God to illuminate is nothing other, than in that manner by his influx to cooperate in such cognitions by which the will is excited.
pass_b_english: Thesis XCIV. For him this illumination of the mind is simply a set of notions received from an external preacher or from some other source, and helped by a special, supernatural influence of God so that they are in some way already fitted for salvation. He observes that when God enlightens people in the ordinary way he does not send into them new species and ideas from which that knowledge arises, the knowledge through whose intervention their minds are enlightened.

That knowledge arises through species acquired in the human way and stirred up by preachers or by some other means. God inserts himself into them by his influence, so that this knowledge becomes more or less fitted for salvation, in proportion as his influence is greater or smaller. On Molina's view, then, for God to enlighten is nothing else than to cooperate in this way, by his influence, in the kinds of knowledge that rouse the will.

lemmas.gloss: does not send in new species and ideas
through species acquired in human manner

choices.why: Molina places the first part of prevenient grace in knowledge helped by God's special influence.

bible_refs: Luis de Molina SJ, Concordia liberi arbitrii cum gratiae donis (Lisbon, 1588), question 14, article 13, disputation 45.
